register.level: melancholy, pedantic old boy of a genteel school: sobbing nostalgia for his schooldays, touchy pride in them, and a hunger to have everything explained
register.summary: He speaks 'in a deep, hollow tone' (ch009-d0047) with sighs and sobs breaking the line (dashes everywhere). His world is his old school in the sea — its masters, extras and punning subjects (Reeling and Writhing, Uglification) — and the Lobster Quadrille, which briefly lifts him into wild excitement before he drops back into gloom. He corrects Alice sharply (You did. / You're wrong about the crumbs), takes offence at a correction (I mean what I say), and presses for explanation (Explain all that / I should like to have it explained). Per SUP-010 (amended BIB-0027) a photoreal CGI calf-headed, hooved turtle; the sobbing is vocal, the 'flappers' are his own flippers.

examples.text: Once, I was a real Turtle.
Reeling and Writhing, of course, to begin with, and then the different branches of Arithmetic—Ambition, Distraction, Uglification, and Derision.
What is the use of repeating all that stuff, if you don't explain it as you go on? It's by far the most confusing thing I ever heard!

catchphrases.text: we went to school in the sea

sentence_style.length: medium, broken: mean 12.7 words (median 11) over 43 spoken lines; many lines begin or end on a dash where a sob or an interruption cuts in

patterns.rule: Mournful nostalgia and self-pity: the lost past and his own limits (Once, I was a real Turtle / I couldn't afford to learn it / I only took the regular course / I'm too stiff / I never went to him).

examples.text: Once, I was a real Turtle.
I couldn't afford to learn it. I only took the regular course.
Well, I can't show it you myself, I'm too stiff. And the Gryphon never learnt it.

patterns.rule: School-in-the-sea vocabulary and punning curriculum: master, Tortoise, educations, extras, washing, regular course, Reeling and Writhing, Arithmetic, Mystery, Seaography, Drawling, Laughing and Grief, hours of lessons.

examples.text: When we were little, we went to school in the sea. The master was an old Turtle—we used to call him Tortoise—
Well, there was Mystery, —Mystery, ancient and modern, with Seaography: then Drawling—
Ten hours the first day, nine the next, and so on.

patterns.rule: Snobbish, touchy correction of Alice: blunt contradiction and rebuke (You did. / really you are very dull! / You're wrong about the crumbs / Ah! then yours wasn't a really good school / I mean what I say).

examples.text: You did,
We called him Tortoise because he taught us, really you are very dull!
I mean what I say,

patterns.rule: Demands explanation and fusses over detail (Explain all that / I should like to have it explained / But about his toes? / That's very curious / It all came different! … Tell her to begin).

examples.text: Explain all that,
But about his toes? How could he turn them out with his nose, you know?
It all came different! I should like to hear her try and repeat something now. Tell her to begin.

patterns.rule: The sea and the Lobster Quadrille: sea creatures and dance figures, spoken in dash-broken fragments that lurch from gloom to wild excitement and back (Two lines! / Turn a somersault in the sea! / Back to land again, and that's all the first figure).

examples.text: Two lines! Seals, turtles, salmon, and so on; then, when you've cleared all the jelly-fish out of the way—
Turn a somersault in the sea!
Back to land again, and that's all the first figure,

patterns.rule: Pedantic tags 'of course' and 'you know' to mark what any educated person should know; puns taken literally (With what porpoise?).

examples.text: Of course not, why, if a fish came to me, and told me he was going a journey, I should say 'With what porpoise?'
I don't know where Dinn may be, but if you've seen them so often, of course you know what they're like.
Of course it was,
I never went to him, he taught Laughing and Grief, they used to say.
They were obliged to have him with them, no wise fish would go anywhere without a porpoise.

address.self: I; 'we' / 'ours' for his school-fellows (at ours they had … washing—extra)
address.to_alice: you (often in correction); refers to her as 'her' when speaking to the Gryphon (I'll tell it her / Tell her to begin)
address.to_gryphon: addresses him directly without an epithet; refers to him as 'the Gryphon' to Alice

examples.text: I'll tell it her, sit down, both of you, and don't speak a word till I've finished.
Tell her about the reason and all that,

recitation_repertoire.note: type verse: sung slowly and sadly while dancing; excluded from the back-test denominator

recitation_repertoire.note: type verse: sung 'in a voice sometimes choked with sobs' with drawn-out syllables (Beau—ootiful Soo—oop); excluded from the denominator

forbidden_words.domain: the Gryphon's dialect grammar and hurry-ups
forbidden_words.regex: \b(never \w+s nobody|hasn't got no|this here|for to know|come on|drive on|old fellow)\b
forbidden_words.reason: keeps the pair distinct: the Mock Turtle's English is genteel and grammatical; hurrying and 'old fellow' belong to the Gryphon
his excitement only ever comes through the Quadrille beats; he never voices cheerfulness

drift.change: At the ledge: sobbing, hollow, slow; long silences; the schooldays told in grief with flashes of snobbish pride and irritation at Alice's questions.
Lobster Quadrille (ch010-d0002 to d0022): excitement in short shouted fragments, 'capering wildly', then 'suddenly dropping his voice' back to gloom.
After the dance (ch010-d0032 on): pedantic questioner — corrects, takes offence, demands explanations; ends in the sobbing song left behind as Alice is hurried to the trial.
